items.originalTitle: Poll: Less than a third of Americans expect the next president to be Republican
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Poll: Less than a third of Americans expect the next president to be Republican
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. We're playing the same electoral map with the same swing states.”

items.originalTitle: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state. Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

items.originalTitle: ‘We want our story to be told’: inside a shocking 36-year fight for justice in Baltimore
items.author: Adrian Horton
items.title: ‘We want our story to be told’: inside a shocking 36-year fight for justice in Baltimore
items.summary: A staggering case of injustice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Ta-Nehisi Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight years old at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and convicted for the murder were the right guys, and the episode faded into one of those strange imprints from the past, a blurry but foundational event.

items.originalTitle: Cornyn links Nvidia scandal to perception of Trump admin corruption
items.author: Casey He
items.title: Cornyn links Nvidia scandal to perception of Trump admin corruption
items.summary: Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn sees the Nvidia scandal and questions about the Trump administration’s alleged lax chip export control rules as part of a broader perception of corruption, which he said contributed to the Republican drubbing in the midterms. “Let’s talk about Nvidia and export controls,” the Texas Republican said when asked to name examples of corruption he sees at the federal level during an onstage interview at the Atlantic Summit on Tuesday. He then pointed to media reports that advanced Nvidia chips may have been diverted to China through the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, and that the Commerce Department, led by Secretary Howard Lutnick, resisted efforts by other Cabinet agencies to crack down on Megaspeed. “I just think there’s a lot of things that will be investigated, and we’ll learn more about, basically, this perception that there was self-dealing going on that I think caused a lot of unease by the American people,” Cornyn said. He said President Donald Trump is at the center of the perceived corruption — “the buck stops with him” — and that many congressional Republicans, fearing the White House’s retribution, have chosen not to cross the president publicly. Cornyn’s remarks come as fallout from the Nvidia turmoil that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster continues to roil Washington. The Trump administration is scrambling to further restrict China’s access to the most advanced American chips as pressure mounts from Capitol Hill, which is also set to hear testimony from Huang and Lutnick in the coming weeks. The four-term senator, who lost his primary earlier this year to the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton, did not mince words when asked about the cause of the blue wave that swept even statewide offices across his home state. “Well, President Trump said he was on the ballot.” In a pair of statements, White House spokespeople blamed Democrats for refusing “to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government” and highlighted the Commerce Department’s interim final rule to “crack down on the smuggling of advanced U.S. SI chips, including through third countries and remote access by Chinese SI labs.” “The Trump Administration will continue to take decisive action to protect America’s technological edge, strengthen our national security, and ensure the future of SI is built in America,” White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton said. Cornyn in his remarks Tuesday also urged Washington to keep China as its top national security and foreign policy focus, as Trump is set to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping later this week. He warned about disruption to the semiconductor supply chain should China try to invade Taiwan, its island democracy neighbor that produces an overwhelming majority of the world’s most advanced chips. “The idea that there could be another pandemic or military conflict or natural disaster that would disrupt that ought to worry everybody,” he said. “That’s one of my principal concerns is what China may or may not do in the Taiwan Straits.”

items.summary: Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger? It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power.
